appraisal_events.evidence: Le Prince a « fait une algarade à Swann et lui a fait assavoir [...] de ne plus avoir à se montrer chez lui, étant donné les opinions qu'il affiche » ; Froberville trouve que « mon oncle Gilbert a eu mille fois raison » d'en finir « avec un dreyfusard avéré » ; le duc juge que « sa conduite à notre égard a été inqualifiable » et énumère ce qu'il croyait de lui : « un fin gourmet, un esprit positif, un collectionneur [...] membre du Jockey [...] qui nous envoyait le meilleur porto qu'on puisse boire ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The Guermantes circle converges on a single act of condemnation and expulsion: Swann is barred from the Prince's house and denounced as a Dreyfusard, losing the patronage the duc recalls having extended to him. The narrator reports the social consequence as real while ironizing the judges, whose grounds for esteem turn out to be porto, the Jockey Club and good addresses.

appraisal_events.evidence: Ruiné et marié à une parente pauvre des Guermantes, il est de « ces gens qu'on laissait de côté, hors des grandes occasions » ; secouru par Mme de Saint-Euverte, « le colonel, qui passait pour un bon garçon, n'avait pas l'âme reconnaissante », « envieux des splendeurs d'une bienfaitrice », au point de « souhaiter que le mauvais temps » fasse rater la fête.
appraisal_events.explanation: Immediately after Froberville pronounces sentence on Swann, the narrator devotes a paragraph to stripping him: socially marginal, materially dependent on charity, and ungratefully envious of his benefactress. The diminishment is directly asserted rather than reported, and it undercuts the authority of the man who has just endorsed Swann's expulsion.

status_effects.explanation: Within the Guermantes world Swann falls sharply in this passage: he is forbidden the Prince's house, his conduct is called inqualifiable by the duc, and the former patronage of the Guermantes and the duc de Chartres is invoked only to measure the fall.
The narrator turns the reputation of a bon garçon inside out, showing him ungrateful and envious of the woman who clothes his daughters, and wishing a storm on her party.
He is placed at the edge of the great world, a once-a-year communicant invited only for large occasions, holding his position through a poor Guermantes wife and Mme de Saint-Euverte's charity.

ambiguities: Bréauté and Froberville give incompatible accounts of the Swann-Gilbert conversation (a bon mot about a Bergotte playlet versus a political expulsion), and Froberville declares Bréauté's version « de tout point controuvée ». The salon's praise of Swann's retort as « très spirituel » is therefore reported at two removes and possibly fabricated, so it is not recorded as a stable countervailing appraisal against the expulsion.

Froberville calls the prince de Guermantes « mon oncle Gilbert » although the narrator has just identified his uncle as the général de Froberville; the kinship claim may be social inflation on his part, which would further weaken his authority as the source of the expulsion story, though the reference of « Gilbert » to the prince de Guermantes is itself secure.
